newsitem.title: USA: Shoplifting, employee theft add to supermarket prices.
newsitem.headline: Shoplifting, employee theft add to supermarket prices.

text.p: Shoplifting and employee theft are costing supermarkets more and more each year -- costs that eventually find their way into consumers' shopping carts.
"Theft is one additional cost that has to be cut ... and it can contribute to higher prices," said Edie Clark, a spokeswoman for the Food Marketing Institute, an industry organisation.
Last year, supermarkets caught about 252,264 shoplifters, averaging about 41 incidents per store, according to a survey of 74 supermarket companies operating more than 11,000 stores.

The value of recovered merchandise topped $8.7 million, averaging $22.57 per incident, according to the survey by the institute. Top theft items included cigarettes at 41 percent and health and beauty items at 36 percent.
In 1995, shoplifters stole about $8 million worth of merchandise, up from $6.5 million in 1994.
It is not clear whether there is more theft overall, or better security leading to more apprehensions, Clark said.

Detected employee theft occurred an average of 2.8 times per store last year, the survey showed, resulting in a total of 18,054 detected incidents. The average value of cash and merchandise recovered per incident was $175.14, with 44 percent of the incidents occuring at checkout and 23 percent occuring in sales and service areas.
In 1995, there were 14,678 detected incidents of employee theft, with an average cache of $193.49, the institute said.
Worthless checks were responsible for a total loss of more than $111 million in 1996, FMI said, with an average of $70.30 per check, up from a total of $70 million lost in 1995.
Clark said that as an industry, supermarkets have a net profit of 1.21 percent, or 1 cent per dollar after taxes.
Theft of a $1 item means that a supermarket has to sell $100 worth to make up the loss, Clark said.

It's no accident that you often leave the grocery store with far more items than you anticipated. Supermarket research shows that the more people see, the more they will buy. Thus, goodies are often displayed at the end of high-traffic aisles and milk and bread, the two things you came in for, are at opposite ends of the store.
Here are some tips to outsmart your supermarket and save money at the same time, offered by Good Housekeeping magazine in its August edition.
Look high and low -- Most expensive brands are placed at eye level. Look at higher or lower shelves for the best bargains.
Search for your favourites -- Grocers sometimes move around items, hoping you'll be tempted to buy other things while trying to locate an item.

Stear clear of trimmings -- Items such as taco fixings are often displayed next to the chopped meat, candy toppings by the ice cream and dip near the chips. Stores often pair popular items with less popular ones hoping you'll be tempted and make a spur-of-the-moment purchase.

Beware of bargains -- A sign that reads "new" or "special" may indicate a product is anything but. A brand in a free-standing display doesn't mean it's a good value. Studies have shown that one-third of shoppers buy from so-called bargain bins thinking they're getting a discount. Best to compare prices.
Don't follow your nose -- Grocers hope the aroma from the bakery section will whet your appetite and lead you to buy more.

Finally, don't get lulled by the slow-tempo mood music playing over the loudspeaker. Upbeat music has been shown to cut sales by 38 percent. Hum your own tune, keep up your pace and keep your spending under control.

The newest look in wedding photography is the photojournalistic style, highlighted by the famous photo by Denis Reggie of John F. Kennedy Jr. kissing the hand of his new bride, Carolyn Bessette, after their 1996 wedding.
"Every shot should have meaning and purpose. Wedding photography should come from the soul," Reggie said in Bride's magazine's August/September issue.
Couples who want to capture their individuality and emotions might consider this new genre of wedding photography. Natural and sophisticated, the photos are more photojournalistic than formal.
"Posing and concocting stances -- that's not reality," Reggie said. "Shots like these should be kept to an absolute minimum."

Finding a photographer well-versed in this modern photo style might take some digging. Bride's suggests asking around, checking out bridal publications for real-life wedding pictures, or contacting the Professional Photographers of America (888-977-8679) for names of photographers in your area who specialise in photojournalistic wedding photos.
As always, check references carefully and make sure to get a contract in writing that specifically states what kind of photos will be taken, how many will be printed and how much the event will cost.
